1.pericope_label: Then said the Lord unto me, Though Moses and Samuel stood before me, yet my mind could not be toward this people: cast them out of my sight, and let them go forth. And it shall come to pass, if they say unto thee, Whither shall we go forth? then thou shalt tell them, Thus saith the Lord; Such as are for death, to death; and such as are for the sword, to the sword. And I will appoint over them four kinds, saith the Lord: the sword to slay, and the dogs to tear, and the fowls of the heaven, and the beasts of the earth, to devour and destroy. And I will cause them to be removed into all kingdoms of the earth, because of Manasseh the son of Hezekiah king of Judah.

schools.summary: Ellicott supplies the setting and the parallels: the anthropomorphism of the refusal, the liturgical sense of standing before God, and the antiquity of the horror at bodies left to dogs and birds.

Gill and Calvin part over how far the removal reaches, Gill running past Babylon to the last captivity and Calvin holding to the exile in view; Calvin also refuses to let the rejected prayer be wasted, since it distinguished the titular church from the chosen seed.
Clarke turns the refusal on the intercessor and makes the present dispersion an argument against unbelief; Wesley reduces the casting out to revulsion, that God cannot abide the sight of them.

Henry measures the refusal from the prophet's side, that not a reprieve was gained though he prayed and others joined him, and holds that Manasseh's sin is reckoned still though a generation had worn off.

debates.question: What does cast them out of my sight mean?

positions.position: Out of the temple courts they profane; to stand before God in this idiom is to minister there.
A prohibition on intercession: do not bring them into my presence by your prayers.
Revulsion: God cannot abide the sight of them.

debates.question: Was the intercession wholly refused?

positions.position: Wholly: not a reprieve was gained, the decree had gone forth and was irreversible.
Refused as to the mass only; the prophet had all along distinguished the titular church from the chosen seed.

debates.question: Do the dogs tear, or drag about?

positions.position: Tear: the second of four instruments of justice following the sword.
Drag about, which is what dogs actually do and carries a more horrid idea.
Four families, or four sorts of punishment, following the Targum.

debates.question: How far does the removal reach?

positions.position: To the exile in view, its grievousness being that they wander in fear with no safe rest.
Past Babylon to the last captivity, or given for a commotion, so they are fugitives like Cain.
To the whole present dispersion, which is itself an argument unbelief cannot answer.

outliers.claim: Observes that the exposure of the dead has been the crowning horror of defeat from the earliest stages of history, and quotes the poet who sent mighty souls to Hades and made their bodies a prey to dogs and to all birds.
Notes that most of a generation had worn off since Manasseh's time and his sin is reckoned in the account still.

themes: Then said the Lord unto me, Though Moses and Samuel stood before me, yet my mind could not be toward this people: cast them out of my sight, and let them go forth.

And it shall come to pass, if they say unto thee, Whither shall we go forth? then thou shalt tell them, Thus saith the Lord; Such as are for death, to death; and such as are for the sword, to the sword; and such as are for the famine, to the famine; and such as are for the captivity, to the captivity.
And I will appoint over them four kinds, saith the Lord: the sword to slay, and the dogs to tear, and the fowls of the heaven, and the beasts of the earth, to devour and destroy.
And I will cause them to be removed into all kingdoms of the earth, because of Manasseh the son of Hezekiah king of Judah, for that which he did in Jerusalem.

5.pericope_label: For who shall have pity upon thee, O Jerusalem? or who shall bemoan thee? or who shall go aside to ask how thou doest? Thou hast forsaken me, saith the Lord, thou art gone backward: therefore will I stretch out my hand against thee, and destroy thee; I am weary with repenting. And I will fan them with a fan in the gates of the land; I will bereave them of children, I will destroy my people, since they return not from their ways. Their widows are increased to me above the sand of the seas. She that hath borne seven languisheth: her sun is gone down while it was yet day.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott divide over the tense, Ellicott making the clauses past and Keil and Delitzsch prophetic, and they charge the past reading to a settled system of slighting prophecy.

Gill measures the refusal of pity by the smallest courtesies and reports the Talmud on the seven kings; Calvin makes the want of any human sympathy the measure of desert, and takes the gates of the earth for all countries.

Clarke reads the gates as the places of public justice and the mother as the metropolis; Wesley keeps strictly to the figure of fanning at barn doors and holds that the prophet speaks of things to come as if present.

debates.question: What does I am weary with repenting mean?

positions.position: Weariness with repeatedly changing his purpose, having often shown mercy after purposing to punish.
He has so often repented that he cannot now be induced to forgive.
A resolve to bear no longer.
Weary of pitying, or of relenting, would be the better rendering.

debates.question: What are the gates of the land?

positions.position: Their own land, or else the enemy's cities, following the Targum.
The places of public justice, from which they go into captivity.
Barn doors, the figure of fanning kept strictly.
The approaches of the land, as men speak of the Cilician gates or the gates of India.
All countries: the gates of the earth, since they thought themselves safe in their own.

debates.question: Should the verbs be past or prophetic?

positions.position: Past: I have winnowed, I have bereaved, I have destroyed.
Prophetic of what is irrevocably determined; the past reading comes of a system of slighting prophecy.
Prediction, though the past is grammatically possible.
The prophet speaks of things to come as if present.

debates.question: Who is the mother of the young men?

positions.position: The metropolis, the mother city.
An actual woman, the mother of the young warrior, on whom travail-pangs fall where the English has a spoiler falling on a city.
The mother that has borne many, weakened by losing the strength her children gave her.

outliers.claim: Suggests that the image of a sun gone down while it was yet day may have been struck out by the total eclipse seen in Palestine in the autumn of the year of Megiddo, as an earthquake once furnished imagery to other prophets.
Records that the Talmud takes the seven children for seven wicked kings, and gives both lists it offers, one of Israel and one of Judah.

themes: For who shall have pity upon thee, O Jerusalem? or who shall bemoan thee? or who shall go aside to ask how thou doest?
Thou hast forsaken me, saith the Lord, thou art gone backward: therefore will I stretch out my hand against thee, and destroy thee; I am weary with repenting.
And I will fan them with a fan in the gates of the land; I will bereave them of children, I will destroy my people, since they return not from their ways.

Their widows are increased to me above the sand of the seas: I have brought upon them against the mother of the young men a spoiler at noonday: I have caused him to fall upon it suddenly, and terrors upon the city.

She that hath borne seven languisheth: she hath given up the ghost; her sun is gone down while it was yet day: she hath been ashamed and confounded: and the residue of them will I deliver to the sword before their enemies, saith the Lord.

10.pericope_label: Woe is me, my mother, that thou hast borne me a man of strife and a man of contention to the whole earth! I have neither lent on usury, nor men have lent to me on usury; yet every one of them doth curse me. The Lord said, Verily it shall be well with thy remnant; verily I will cause the enemy to entreat thee well in the time of evil. Shall iron break the northern iron and the steel? Thy substance and thy treasures will I give to the spoil without price, and that for all thy sins, even in all thy borders. And I will make thee to pass with thine enemies into a land which thou knowest not.

schools.summary: Ellicott suspects dislocation, counts the rival readings of the iron question before choosing one, and suspects the closing verse corrupt; Keil and Delitzsch see no dislocation and work the grammar of the two irons.

Gill insists the treasures are the people's and not the prophet's, and offers both the comforting and the political sense of the iron; Calvin bounds the outburst as restrained weakness and reads the borders metaphorically for counsels.
Clarke points past the wording to the event, the Babylonian king's charge that Jeremiah be looked to; Wesley takes the remnant for the remnant of days he had left to live.
Henry sets the scene, the prophet returned from public work into his closet and afterwards publishing what passed there, and marks that a man who provoked none was a man of strife notwithstanding.

debates.question: Do these verses stand in their right place?

positions.position: No: a fragment merged into the chapter's artificial continuity, better placed after the fourteenth verse.
Yes: the shifts of address are explained by complaint and answer both bearing on the people.

debates.question: Is the outburst a lapse?

positions.position: A man of like passions wishing he had never been born, and seeming to blame his mother.
Weakness genuinely felt, but restrained by the Spirit from breaking out intemperately.
The apostrophe measures the depth of the sorrow rather than reproaching her.
A peaceable man who provoked none and was a man of strife notwithstanding.

debates.question: What does it shall be well with thy remnant mean?

positions.position: The remnant of days Jeremiah had left to live.
I afflict thee for thy good, the reading being uncertain among three proposals.
I strengthen thee for thy good.
Read from the event: the Babylonian king charged that Jeremiah be looked to and granted what he asked.

debates.question: What does the iron question mean?

positions.position: That the prophet's prayer cannot change an inflexible purpose to chastise.
That the Jews, hard as iron, could not prevail against a prophet made an iron pillar.
That weak forces cannot oppose the Chaldean power, God having hardened them.
A question of construing the two irons, the simile of one iron breaking another being unnatural.

outliers.claim: Sets out four rival readings of the iron question that he refuses — Judah's powerlessness against the Chaldeans, the impotence of the prophet's enemies, his own want of power against the people's obduracy, and the weakness of one king against another — before choosing a fifth.
Doubts that the borders of the land can be meant and reads the word metaphorically for counsels or ends, quoting a heathen poet on there being something a man goes toward and levels his bow at.

themes: Woe is me, my mother, that thou hast borne me a man of strife and a man of contention to the whole earth! I have neither lent on usury, nor men have lent to me on usury; yet every one of them doth curse me.
The Lord said, Verily it shall be well with thy remnant; verily I will cause the enemy to entreat thee well in the time of evil and in the time of affliction.
Shall iron break the northern iron and the steel?
Thy substance and thy treasures will I give to the spoil without price, and that for all thy sins, even in all thy borders.
And I will make thee to pass with thine enemies into a land which thou knowest not: for a fire is kindled in mine anger, which shall burn upon you.

15.pericope_label: O Lord, thou knowest: remember me, and visit me, and revenge me of my persecutors; take me not away in thy longsuffering: know that for thy sake I have suffered rebuke. Thy words were found, and I did eat them; and thy word was unto me the joy and rejoicing of mine heart: for I am called by thy name, O Lord God of hosts. I sat not in the assembly of the mockers, nor rejoiced; I sat alone because of thy hand: for thou hast filled me with indignation. Why is my pain perpetual, and my wound incurable, which refuseth to be healed? wilt thou be altogether unto me as a liar, and as waters that fail?

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch locate the pain in the message rather than in the hostility it draws, and explain the loneliness by the hand that laid hold on the prophet; Ellicott corrects the mockers to the mirthful and the liar to a winter torrent.

Gill allows the pain both senses and extends the eating of the words to his own readers; Calvin reads the abrupt turn to God as a device rather than a collapse, and makes the assembly a council of wicked rulers.

Clarke takes the prayer literally, as a plea not to be carried into captivity, and reaches for the desert mirage; Wesley glosses the visiting as love and makes the whole prophetic life a time of mourning and solitude.

Henry finds the comfort of having a God to go to before whom the case may be spread and the omniscience appealed to, and reads the petition as asking both remembrance and the strength that a visit brings.

debates.question: Is the complaint a collapse or a device?

positions.position: Real bitterness: not even the promise has given him rest, and the words recall the imprecations of the so-called vindictive psalms.
A deliberate device: the abrupt turn from people to God has more force than calm and uniform order.
Simply that a great prophet was, like Elijah, a man of like passions with other men.

debates.question: What is asked in remember me and visit me?

positions.position: That God consider his case and communicate strength and comfort.
Literal preservation from being carried into captivity.
Nothing beyond the opening word: God knew his heart, his innocence, his afflictions and his enemies' designs.

debates.question: Who sat in the assembly he stayed away from?

positions.position: The mirthful rather than the mockers; the word behind the name meaning laughter needs no cynical sense.
A council of wicked rulers, the word also meaning a secret conclave.
The company matters less than the cause: the hand of God had laid hold on him.

debates.question: What is the perpetual pain?

positions.position: Grief at the judgment he must announce, expressly not the hostility he endures for announcing it.
Both: the uneasiness for his people and the pain his persecutors gave him.

outliers.claim: Reads the waters that fail as the desert mirage, where an action of the air on rising vapours makes the resemblance of water, and the traveller rejoices he has reached a lake that keeps its distance and at last vanishes.
Corrects the English on being called by thy name: more literally the Name is called upon him, the witness of his special consecration.

themes: O Lord, thou knowest: remember me, and visit me, and revenge me of my persecutors; take me not away in thy longsuffering: know that for thy sake I have suffered rebuke.
Thy words were found, and I did eat them; and thy word was unto me the joy and rejoicing of mine heart: for I am called by thy name, O Lord God of hosts.
I sat not in the assembly of the mockers, nor rejoiced; I sat alone because of thy hand: for thou hast filled me with indignation.
Why is my pain perpetual, and my wound incurable, which refuseth to be healed? wilt thou be altogether unto me as a liar, and as waters that fail?

19.pericope_label: Therefore thus saith the Lord, If thou return, then will I bring thee again, and thou shalt stand before me: and if thou take forth the precious from the vile, thou shalt be as my mouth: let them return unto thee; but return not thou unto them. And I will make thee unto this people a fenced brasen wall: and they shall fight against thee, but they shall not prevail against thee: for I am with thee to save thee and to deliver thee, saith the Lord. And I will deliver thee out of the hand of the wicked, and I will redeem thee out of the hand of the terrible.

schools.summary: Ellicott turns the sifting of precious from vile inward on the prophet and marks that the renewed promise reproduces the words of his call, resting on conditions he had imperfectly fulfilled; Keil and Delitzsch describe the answer as reprimand and renewed assurance.

Gill takes the promise as a direct answer to the charge that God had been as a liar; Calvin explains why the complaint was published at all, and flags a suspected corruption at one word before refusing to act on it.
Clarke reports the older reading of a return to his own country before setting it aside, and closes on the fulfilment; Wesley makes the answer a rebuke of distrust and an order to keep his ground.

debates.question: Whom does If thou return address, and to what?

positions.position: The prophet, called back from the unbelief he has just expressed.
The prophet, rebuked for distrust, with restoration to his former standing attached.
The prophet, who needs to return to his true mind no less than the people do.
Reported first as returning by repentance to his own country, then set aside for his ministry.
An answer in two motions: reprimand of his impatience, and renewed assurance of protection.

debates.question: What is the precious and the vile he must separate?

positions.position: The people's deceitful words against the message given him.
God's precious truths against the vile conceits of men.
His own righteous zeal against the despondent bitterness that counterfeits it.

debates.question: Does the renewed promise answer the charge that God had been as a liar?

positions.position: Directly: it is what was promised at his call, so God was no liar to him after all.
Yes, but it rested on implied conditions the desponding prophet had imperfectly fulfilled.
Conditionally: while thou art faithful to me, none shall prevail.
As encouragement to a man alone under a burden too heavy for him.

debates.question: Who are the wicked and the terrible?

positions.position: The Jews who imprisoned him, the king and his courtiers.
That evil people's power, and then the Chaldean armies.
A confirmation that adds strength sufficient to deliver to the earlier promise of presence.

outliers.claim: Explains why the complaint was published at all: had the prophet spoken only from the heroic elevation of his own mind, the proud of this world would have derided him as hardhearted or a fanatic, so he set out his own infirmity and thereby proved the people guilty rather than himself weak.
Names the temptation the order guards against — that a sense of failure might send the prophet back to the people in the temper of a man who tunes his voice according to the time.

themes: Therefore thus saith the Lord, If thou return, then will I bring thee again, and thou shalt stand before me: and if thou take forth the precious from the vile, thou shalt be as my mouth: let them return unto thee; but return not thou unto them.

And I will make thee unto this people a fenced brasen wall: and they shall fight against thee, but they shall not prevail against thee: for I am with thee to save thee and to deliver thee, saith the Lord.
And I will deliver thee out of the hand of the wicked, and I will redeem thee out of the hand of the terrible.
